title: Async IO spike coupling across SKUs: notes and matrix
content:
Summary:

Quick notes from experiments comparing asynchronous IO and request spike coupling across A100/H100/L40S cloud SKUs and multiple driver/CUDA combinations. Goal: isolate whether observed per-token jitter and occasional 5-15x p99 spikes originate in host-side IO queueing, GPU kernel contention, or NVLink/PCIe coupling when multiple workstreams hit the device simultaneously.

Why this felt urgent:
- We saw a customer-reported p99 tail regression on long-context chat workloads after a provider driver update (reports started 2025-08).
- Prior benches focused on raw prefill/decode throughput; less coverage on asynchronous host IO patterns and cross-stream coupling.
- Hypothesis: async prefetch + multi-stream kernel launch fanout creates short-lived bursts that amplify driver/firmware serialization or PCIe link state transitions on specific SKUs.

Experiment matrix (high level):
- Hardware SKUs: AWS p4d (A100-80GB), GCP a2-megagpu (A100-40GB), GCP h1/highmem-H100 (H100-80GB equiv), Azure L40s prod sku (L40S).
- Driver/CUDA variants: cuda-11.8 + nvidia-525.x, cuda-12.1 + nvidia-535.x, cuda-12.2 + nvidia-545.x (where available).
- Models: small GPT-like 1.3B (for high qps), medium 7B, and large 70B half-precision baseline.
- Workloads: synthetic spike pattern (baseline 200 qps into many short requests, plus scheduled 5000 qps 200ms spike every 60s), long-context chat prefill+decode traces recreated from production trace sample, and KV-warmup-dominant workload (large prefill then decode).
- Topology variants: single-GPU instance, multi-GPU (NVLink enabled where available), single-socket multi-process vs multi-thread runtime, with and without host-side async prefetch thread pool.
- Observability: eBPF for syscall/queue timing (host-side), NVML sampling at 250ms, kernel launch counts from runtime tracing, nsight systems traces for 1s windows around spikes.

Instrumentation notes (how we measured):
- Host: capture write()/read() latencies from prefetch threads with eBPF tracepoints; measure submit latency to GPU driver using ioctl tracepoints where possible.
- Device: NVML GPU utilization, PCIe throughput counters, nvlink counters (via nvidia-smi topo and NVML queries), kernel launch timestamps via CUPTI where supported.
- Runtime: added micro-timestamps at prefill pipeline stages (request receive, queue enqueue, async fetch start/end, kernel enqueue, decode start/end).
- Keep all clocks in monotonic ns; post-process align using trace correlation tags.

Key observations (summary):
1) A100 instances (both 40/80 variants) show frequent sub-200ms jitter but rarely >2x spikes for our medium workloads. P99 generally explained by queueing at the runtime when prefill batches accumulate.

2) H100 instances exhibited the most surprising behavior: occasional 1.5-3s p99 spikes on medium and large models, correlated with short bursts of kernel launch fanout across contexts. These align with moments where nvlink health counters register a brief reduction in usable link bandwidth (observed via NVML on GCP H100 SKUs).

3) L40S instances show stable average latency but a distinct pattern where p95->p99 increases when host CPU interrupts burst (high syscall rates) — suggests host-side scheduling/interrupt handling interacting with PCIe DMA stalls.

4) Driver/CUDA combos matter: on one H100 + cuda-12.1 + nvidia-535.x combo we saw significantly higher kernel launch serialization compared to cuda-12.2 + nvidia-545.x. Upgrading to 12.2 reduced spike frequency by ~60% in repeatable synthetic spike tests. (Cross-validate before rolling out.)

Deeper trace examples (typical spike trace):
- t=0 base: normal prefill -> kernel launch for prefills in small batches.
- t=~85s: synthetic 200ms high qps spike injected. host prefetch threads issue ~8x concurrent DMA submissions per GPU.
- t=~85.01s: nvlink bandwidth drops by 20% momentarily; kernel launch latency queue increases => kernel start delayed by 500-1200ms.
- t=~85.02-85.05s: runtime packs extra decode batches due to backpressure; many kernel completions arrive clustered, creating a short-lived telemetry spike.
- t=~86s: system recovers, but p99 for that second is large.

Root cause hypotheses (not mutually exclusive):
- NVLink transient behavior on some H100 firmware revisions under bursty DMA patterns. Firmware may throttle link briefly during certain transaction mixes.
- Driver-side kernel serialization when many small kernels are submitted concurrently from distinct CUDA streams/contexts; some driver versions perform a conservative serialization to avoid deadlocks.
- Host-side async IO thread pool management: if the pool threads align on a cpu hot-spot, SYSENTER/SYSCALL bursts and interrupts can cause short scheduling latencies, magnified on L40S by platform interrupt routing.

Quick data points pointing to primary causes:
- NVLink counters dip concurrent with spikes on H100, not on A100.
- CUPTI shows increased kernel queuing latency on older driver combos; newer driver reduces queue time.
- eBPF host traces show that when prefetch threads are spread across distinct cores (affinity), spikes reduce on L40S by ~40%—indicating scheduling impact.

Mitigations we tested and short results:
- Staggered prefetch scheduling (add jitter to async prefetch start times): reduced amplitude of jet-like spikes but increased average latency slightly (p50 unchanged, p99 down 30%).
- Collapsing small kernels into fused kernels (runtime-level opcode batching) removed a large fraction of driver serialization on H100; tradeoff: slight throughput drop for some small models due to fusion overhead.
- Updating driver/CUDA (to cuda-12.2 + nvidia-545.x) on H100 reduced NVML-observed kernel queuing; still need vendor confirmation on link throttling bug.
- CPU affinity pinning for prefetch threads: significant win on L40S instances in our lab (requires careful placement across sockets).

Operational recommendations (if we need to ship guidance quickly):
- Avoid aggressive synchronous burst patterns on H100 SKUs until driver/firmware combination validated; prefer staged ramp-ups for large request spikes.
- Default runtime config: add small randomized jitter (1-3ms) to prefetch thread start times when qps > 200 to avoid coherent bursting across threads. Make this adaptive and toggleable via route-level config.
- When upgrading driver across fleet: run a targeted canary that reproduces our synthetic spike pattern at reduced scale to detect serialization regressions. Add NVML and CUPTI sampling to canary checks.
- For L40S, add CPU-affinity recommendations to deployment docs and a small runtime helper to optionally pin prefetch threads to less-interrupt-heavy cores.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Need vendor confirmation on NVLink transient throttle behavior on H100 firmware observed (file ticket with NVIDIA).
- Re-run same tests on multi-tenant noisy host to confirm whether multi-tenant GPU interference amplifies the effect. (Quick test flagged for next week).
- Investigate whether changing GPU context reuse (single context + multiple CUDA streams) vs multiple contexts reduces driver-side serialization in prod runtime.
- Add a small eBPF-based in-prod tail detector that correlates syscall bursts with p99 events for faster diagnosis.

Action items (next 2 weeks):
- Diego: open vendor ticket with NVML traces + nsight snippets (blocked: need sanitized trace for customer).
- Jonah: prototype jittered prefetch option (config flag + small eval harness). Measure perf/quality tradeoffs across 1.3B/7B models.
- Maya: coordinate driver-canary runs on a small fleet slice; collect CUPTI + NVML samples and upload to S3.

Notes to self / rough ideas:
- Could we proactively detect when host prefetch threads align (all start within same 1ms window) and automatically inject stagger? cheap mitigation.
- Consider adding a lightweight kernel coalescer in runtime (attempt to merge tiny decode kernels that are <= Xms execution). Works well for small models; need benchmark for 70B decode pattern.

Appendix (quick config snippets tried):
- runtime flag: --prefetch-jitter-ms=2  (reduced spikes, no user visible regressions in ~24h run)
- runtime rollout checklist for driver upgrade: canary size 5 instances, workload spike generator at 50% of production qps, CUPTI sampling 100ms windows around triggered spikes.

References and traces (local s3 paths):
- s3://redwood-bench/traces/h100/nvml-dump-20250918-1.tar.gz
- s3://redwood-bench/traces/l40s/ebpf-syscall-20250919-1.tar.gz

End notes: this is draft. lots of rough data here but direction is clear: coupling between bursty async IO and device/driver/link behaviors explains many of the p99 anomalies. Prioritize conservative runtime mitigations + driver canary before wholesale fleet driver upgrades.

-- Maya
